source_text: Nescio si quid amplius ad controversiam Baptismi ventilatur. Sane retexam, quod supra omisi, ne imminentes sensus videar intercidere. Unus omnino baptismus est nobis, tam ex Domini Evangelio, quam ex Apostoli litteris; quoniam unus Dominus et unum Baptismum et una Ecclesia in coelis. Sed circa haereticos sane quid custodiendum sit, digne quis retractet; ad nos enim editum est. Haeretici autem nullum habent consortium nostrae disciplinae, quos extraneos utique testatur ipsa ademptio communicationis. Non debeo in illis agnoscere quod mihi est praeceptum, quia non idem Deus est nobis et illis, nec unus Christus, id est idem. Ideoque nec Baptismus unus, quia non idem. Quem cum rite non habeant, sine dubio non habent, nec capit numerari, quod non habetur: ita nec possunt accipere, quia non habent. Sed de isto plenius jam nobis in graeco digestum est. Semel ergo lavacrum inimus, semel delicta diluuntur, quia ea iterari non oportet. Caeterum Israel Judaeus quotidie lavat, quia quotidie inquinatur. Quod ne in nobis quoque factitaretur, propterea de uno lavacro definitum est. Felix aqua quae semel abluit, quae ludibrio pescatoribus non est, quae non assiduitate sordium infecta, rursus, quos diluit, inquinat.
pass_a_gloss: I do not know if anything more is brought forward concerning the controversy of Baptism. Certainly, I will reexamine what I omitted above, lest I seem to cut off impending senses. There is one Baptism for us, both from the Lord's Gospel and from the Apostle's letters; since there is one Lord and one Baptism and one Church in heaven. But what ought to be observed concerning heretics, someone may worthily consider; for it has been decreed to us. Heretics, however, have no sharing in our discipline, whom the very removal of communion indeed testifies as strangers. I ought not to recognize in them what has been commanded to me, because God is not the same for us and for them, nor is Christ the same, that is, the same one. And therefore, neither is Baptism the same, because it is not the same. Which, when they do not have rightly, they certainly do not have, nor can it be counted, what is not had: thus neither can they receive, because they do not have. But concerning this, it has already been more fully discussed by us in Greek. Therefore, we undergo the washing once, sins are washed away once, because it is not fitting to repeat them. Meanwhile, the Jewish Israelite washes daily, because he is defiled daily. Lest this also be done in us, therefore, it has been defined concerning one washing. Happy is the water that washes once, which is not a mockery to fishermen, which, not infected by the frequency of filth, again, does not defile those whom it washes.
pass_b_english: I'm not sure there's anything left to air in the baptism debate, but I'll backtrack and cover what I skipped earlier so I don't look like I'm ducking the implications. There is exactly one baptism for us — grounded in the Lord's Gospel and the apostles' letters — because there is one Lord, one baptism, and one Church in heaven. But what rules apply to heretics? That's a fair question, since the call was handed to us. Heretics have zero share in our discipline; the very fact that we've cut communion with them brands them as outsiders. I'm not about to recognize in them what was commanded to me, because they don't worship the same God we do, nor the same Christ — that is, the identical one. So their baptism isn't the same either, because the source isn't the same. Since they don't have it rightly, they flat-out don't have it; you can't count what isn't there, and they can't receive what they don't possess. We've already hashed this out at length in Greek. The bottom line: we go through the washing once, sins are washed away once, because repeating it is out of the question. Meanwhile, the Jewish Israelite scrubs up daily because he gets dirty daily. To keep that cycle from infecting us, the rule was locked in: one washing. Happy the water that cleanses once and for all — no joke to fishermen, not fouled by constant grime, never turning around and re-defiling the very people it just washed.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A is a faithful literal translation. Pass B is a fluent rendering that preserves all theological nuances, including the causal relations (e.g., 'because the source isn't the same' for 'quia non idem' and 'to keep that cycle from infecting us' for 'Quod ne in nobis quoque factitaretur'). No omissions or additions of meaning were found.
source: 'Nescio si quid amplius ad controversiam Baptismi ventilatur.', English: 'I do not know if anything more is brought forward concerning the controversy of Baptism.'
